title: What if a brand is an RL environment?
subtitle: Part one. We asked a new model to start a cloud kitchen from nothing. Pam's Kitchen came back. This is the whole thing, step by step.

content.text: Let me start with a dog.
You want the dog to sit.
You say "sit."
The dog does something random.
It spins. It barks. It sits.
The moment it sits, you give it a treat.
Do this fifty times.
Now the dog sits when you say "sit."
Nobody explained sitting to the dog.
Nobody wrote a sitting manual.
The dog tried things.
The world told it what worked.
That is reinforcement learning.
RL, for short.
It is how a lot of today's best AI got good.
Not by reading more.
By trying things inside a world.
And getting told, again and again, what worked.
The world has a name in RL.
It is called the environment.
The pieces are simple.
There is an agent. That is the dog.
There is an environment. That is your living room.
The agent sees the state of the room.
It takes an action.
The environment answers with a reward.
A treat, or no treat.
Then it all repeats.
One full run is called an episode.
The rulebook the agent builds up is called a policy.
A policy is just a habit.
"When I hear sit, I sit."
Coding models got scary good this way.
The environment is a codebase.
The action is a code change.
The reward is simple.
Did the tests pass?
Maths models too.
The action is a proof.
The reward is whether the answer is right.
Those worlds are clean.
Tests pass or fail.
Answers are right or wrong.
So the question I keep chewing on is simple.
What if a brand is an environment too?
Think about what a brand actually is.
It is a world with rules.
A name. A voice. Colours. A promise.
Customers walk through it.
They react to every move you make.
They buy, or they scroll past.
That is a state.
That is an action.
That is a reward.
The catch is the reward.
In code, the reward is crisp.
In brands, the reward is messy.
Sales are slow.
Sales are noisy.
Sales depend on weather, payday and luck.
And there is a nastier problem.
If you only reward clicks, you get slop.
Shouting headlines.
Fake discounts.
Stock photos of smiling people holding salads.
The internet is already full of this.
Every AI tool can make more of it.
Fast. Cheap. Forever.
So the real question has two halves.
Can an RL-style setup build a brand that looks good?
Not sloppy. Not generic.
Something with a creative bend.
And can that same brand actually move sales?
Most people pick one.
Taste people make beautiful things that never sell.
Growth people make ugly things that sell for a week.
I want both.
I think the only way to get both is to design the environment.
Not the ad. Not the logo.
The world the agent works inside.
Why do I keep saying world, and not prompt?
A prompt is a note you hand someone once.
"Make me a flyer for a kitchen."
They make one.
Then they forget everything.
The next prompt starts from zero.
A world sticks around.
It has rules that apply every time.
It remembers what got killed last week.
It knows the price, the voice and the colours.
It knows which words are banned.
Prompts are like shouting directions at a stranger.
An environment is like moving into a house.
The house shapes how you live.
You stop thinking about where the kitchen is.
You just cook.
Most AI brand work today is prompt work.
That is why it looks the same.
Everyone is shouting the same directions.
At the same stranger.
So we ran a test.
The Sloosh team post-trained a new model.
We wanted to see how far it could go alone.
We gave it one job.
Start a new cloud kitchen company.
That's it.
No brand book.
No designer.
No list of dishes.
It came back with Pam's Kitchen.
A homemade Indian dark kitchen.
A name. A ritual. A website.
App listings. Five flyers. A pamphlet.
A coffee-table book. T-shirts.
Forty-odd pieces.
All of them agree with each other.
That last part is the real test.
Making one nice image is easy now.
Any tool can do it.
Making forty pieces that feel like one brand is hard.
That is where slop usually shows up.
Piece twelve drifts.
Piece thirty forgets the voice.
By piece forty, it's a different company.
So how do you stop the drift?
This is how you break it down.
You start with nothing.
Then you lay on top of that the right skill files.
Then the models.
Then the workflows.
Then the brand sections.
Then the insights.
Then the guides.
Then the methodologies.
Then your own taste.
Then you put it together.
Each layer is part of the environment.
None of them is the brand.
Together they make a world where good brands are easy.
And slop is hard.
Let me walk through what that looked like for a kitchen.
Start with nothing.
Nothing is not empty, though.
Nothing is the mess you already have.
For Pam's Kitchen, the mess was three menus.

attrs.alt: The before. Three menus, three looks.

content.text: The before. Three menus, three looks.
One was a WhatsApp menu card.
Cartoon fonts. Clip-art bowls.
One was a 150-dish list.
Every dish ever. Tiny text.
One was a weekly planner.
Tables. Colours. Prices everywhere.
Each one sort of worked.
Together they said one thing.
"We don't know who we are yet."
That is normal.
Every small food business starts this way.
You cook first.
You brand later.
In RL terms, this is the starting state.
And the starting state tells you a lot.
The 150-dish list was the loudest signal.
Too many choices.
Customers freeze.
Kitchens burn out.
Food gets wasted.
An agent looking at this state has a huge action space.
It could redesign 150 dishes.
It could make 150 photos.
It could write 150 descriptions.
That is the trap.
A huge action space is where slop breeds.
The model spreads itself thin.
Everything gets a little bit of attention.
Nothing gets enough.
So the first real move was a cut.
One pot a day.
Lock it tonight.
The menu went from 150 dishes to one pot.
Order whenever became lock by 9pm.
Cook everything became cook only what's locked.
I love this move.
It is a brand move and an RL move at once.
As a brand move, it creates a ritual.
Scarcity feels special.
When the pot is empty, it's gone.
As an operations move, it kills waste.
You cook what's locked.
Nothing more.
As an RL move, it shrinks the action space.
Now the agent does not design 150 things.
It designs one daily pot really well.
Then it repeats.
Smaller action space.
Faster learning.
Less room for slop.
Why start with a cloud kitchen at all?
Because it is a great first environment.
The episodes are short.
One pot, one day.
You know by 9pm how many people locked.
That is a fast reward for a brand.
The cost of a bad episode is small.
A pot that nobody locks is a lesson.
Not a bankruptcy.
The customer is close.
They message you on WhatsApp.
They tell you the dal was too salty.
That feedback is gold for an agent.
Compare that to a car brand.
Or a bank.
Their episodes take years.
Their mistakes cost millions.
You would not train a dog on a motorway.
You train it in the living room.
A kitchen is the living room of brands.
This is the first big lesson.
Before you add anything, cut.
The best environments are small.
Now the layers.
The first layer is skill files.
A skill file is a short document.
It teaches an agent how to do one thing well.
How to write a menu line.
How to light a food photo.
How to lay out an A5 flyer.
Think of it as the house rules on the fridge.
Every flatmate reads them.
Nobody has to argue every week.
For a kitchen, the skills were things like these.
Write a dish in one line.
Shoot food on steel, never on white plates.
Keep prices in the headline.
Never write "authentic flavours."
That last one matters more than you think.
"Authentic flavours" is the smell of slop.
Every curry house in the world says it.
Banning it forces the agent to say something real.
The second layer is models.
Different models are good at different things.
One writes well.
One makes great food photos.
One is good at layouts.
One is good at checking the others.
In RL terms, these are your actors.
And one of them is your critic.
People skip the critic.
That is a mistake.
The critic is the cheapest taste you can buy.
It looks at every output and asks one question.
"Would this embarrass us?"
The third layer is workflows.
A workflow is an order of operations.
What happens first.
What feeds into what.
Where a human looks.
For Pam's Kitchen, the order went roughly like this.
Ritual first. Name second.
Then the menu.
Then the site.
Then the print.
Then the book.
Then the merch.
Ritual before name sounds backwards.
It isn't, though.
The name has to carry the ritual.
"Pam's Kitchen" sounds like a person.
A real home cook.
That fits a homemade pot that drops daily.
A clever tech name would have fought the ritual.
Order matters in RL too.
It is called a curriculum.
You teach easy things first.
Then harder things that build on them.
A dog learns sit before it learns fetch.
The fourth layer is brand sections.
This is the brand book, split into parts.
Voice. Colour. Type. Photography. Price. Story.
Each section is a constraint.
Constraints sound like the enemy of creativity.
In practice, they are the opposite.
A blank page is terrifying.
A page with three rules is a game.
Pam's Kitchen got a few simple rules.
Bottle green and ghee cream.
Warm serif headlines.
Steel tiffins and kraft boxes.
Real-looking food, never glossy.
A little cheeky. Never mean.
Every later piece had to pass these rules.
That is how forty pieces end up looking like one.
The fifth layer is insights.
Insights are things you know about real people.
They do not come from the model.
They come from life.
A few insights shaped this kitchen.
Indian students in London miss home food.
Their mums worry they don't eat properly.
Londoners love a crispy galette.
Nobody wants to pick from 150 dishes on a Tuesday.
People screenshot things that feel like a note from a friend.
Each insight is a little map.
It tells the agent where the reward probably is.
Watch what happens when insight meets action.

attrs.alt: On the apps. "If you like a crispy galette."

content.text: On the apps. "If you like a crispy galette."
Masala dosa, £3.50.
"If you like a crispy galette."
That line does a lot of work.
It translates an Indian dish into a word Londoners already love.
No explaining.
Just a bridge.
No model invents that line from nothing.
It comes from an insight about who is ordering.
The model's job is to use it well.
Look at the photos on those app screens too.
Same green backdrop.
Same steel plates.
Same soft light.
On a delivery app, you sit in a list of fifty kitchens.
Fifty thumbnails fighting for one thumb.
Most of them look random.
One dish on a white plate.
The next on a wooden board.
The next under a yellow kitchen light.
Pam's looks like one brand in every tile.
That sameness is a feature.
It is how a tiny kitchen looks bigger than it is.
The model did not choose that consistency.
The brand sections forced it.
Every photo had to pass the same three rules.
Green, steel, soft light.
The rules did the branding.
The model just followed them, very fast.
The sixth layer is guides.
Guides are worked examples.
Good ones and bad ones.
"Write like this. Never like that."
Guides are how you show taste to a model.
You cannot describe taste in a rule.
You can only point at it.
For the menu, the guide was a set of one-line dish stories.
Paneer butter masala. The one Delhi made famous.
Rajma masala. Sunday lunch in Delhi.
Aloo paratha. The Punjabi breakfast that lasts till lunch.
Idli. The batter that rises overnight.
Medu vada. The savoury doughnut.

attrs.alt: The menu, by region, with a one-line story for every dish.

content.text: The menu, by region, with a one-line story for every dish.
A dish name tells you what it is.
A one-line story tells you why you want it.
"The savoury doughnut" sells medu vada in four words.
Once the model saw ten of these, it could write a hundred.
That is the power of a guide.
It moves the agent's policy without a single rule.
Guides also teach exploration.
RL has a classic tension.
Exploration versus exploitation.
Do you try something new?
Or repeat what already works?
Too much exploiting, and every flyer looks the same.
Too much exploring, and nothing looks like a brand.
The guides set the balance.
Some examples were safe.
A clean photo. A price. A QR code.
Some were wild on purpose.
Recipes smuggled out in a tin of ghee.
A kitchen with no door.
The wild ones told the model it was allowed to play.
The safe ones told it where home was.
The best pieces sit right between.
Weird enough to remember.
Clear enough to order from.
The seventh layer is methodologies.
Methodology is how you judge the work.
How you score it.
How you decide what ships.
This is where RL gets real.
Because this is the reward.
The honest problem with brands is the reward is slow.
A sale happens days after the flyer.
A repeat order happens weeks later.
Love for a brand happens over years.
RL people call this a sparse reward.
The treat comes so rarely the dog gets confused.
Was it the sit? The bark? The spin?
So you add dense rewards.
Small signals that show up fast.
Signals that point toward the big one.
For a cloud kitchen, the dense signals are easy to list.
Did people lock tomorrow's pot by 9pm?
How many locks per WhatsApp message?
Did they come back next week?
Did anyone screenshot the flyer?
Did anyone forward the pamphlet?
And then the critic's score.
Is it on brand?
Is it specific?
Would a home cook be proud of it?
The critic needs its own little rubric.
Five questions is plenty.
Could any other kitchen have said this?
If yes, it's too generic. Kill it.
Is there a real detail in it?
A dish, a time, a price, a place.
Does it sound like a person?
Or like a brochure?
Does it point at the ritual?
One pot a day. Lock it tonight.
Would we be embarrassed to hand it to a neighbour?
If yes, kill it. No debate.
Five questions.
They take a model two seconds.
They catch most slop before a human sees it.
That saves the human's taste for the hard calls.
The sparse reward is still the boss.
Sales. Repeat sales. Margin.
The dense rewards are the breadcrumbs that lead there.
The trick is to never let a breadcrumb become the goal.
Because that is how slop happens.
RL has a name for this.
Reward hacking.
The agent finds a cheap way to get the treat.
Without doing the real thing.
A dog learns that looking cute also gets treats.
So it stops sitting and just looks cute.
A brand agent rewarded on clicks learns the same trick.
Shout louder.
Fake urgency.
Fifty percent off forever.
Glossy stock curry.
"Authentic flavours."
Clicks go up.
The brand goes down.
Customers stop trusting it.
Sales follow, a little later.
So the methodology needs two kinds of checks.
Checks that reward the right things.
And checks that punish the cheap tricks.
For Pam's Kitchen, the punish list was short and strict.
No fake discounts.
No stock photos.
No "authentic", no "delicious", no "mouth-watering."
No curry clichés in the type.
No price games.
That price line is my favourite rule.
Most food brands hide the price.
Pam's puts it in the headline.
"A home-cooked pot drops every day. It's £4.99."

attrs.alt: The hero. The price is in the headline.

content.text: The hero. The price is in the headline.
Cheap but homemade is the pitch.
Hiding it would be a small lie.
Small lies are where slop starts.
The eighth layer is your own taste.
This is the layer people want to skip.
They hope the model has taste built in.
It sort of does.
It has the average taste of the internet.
Which is exactly the problem.
The average of the internet is slop.
Your taste is the part that is not average.
In RL language, your taste is the reward model.
It is the thing that says "yes, more of this."
And "no, never again."
You don't need to do all the work.
You need to do the judging.
The loop looks like this.
The model makes twenty versions.
The critic kills most of them.
A human looks at the last few.
The human picks one.
Sometimes the human kills all of them.
Then the guide gets one more example.
Next round starts smarter.
AI makes two hundred drafts.
A human kills one hundred and ninety-seven.
That ratio is the whole game.
Generation is cheap now.
Judgement is the scarce thing.
Every time you kill a draft, you teach the environment.
Every kill becomes a new line in a guide.
Every guide line moves the policy.
The next round is a little less sloppy.
That is RL with a human holding the treats.
Let me trace how one piece moves through every layer.
Roughly, it goes like this.
Take the "your mum called" flyer.
It starts with nothing.
A blank A5.
The skill file says how A5 flyers work.
One headline. A short story. One action. A p.s.
The model drafts twenty stories.
Most are fine.
Fine is the enemy.
The insight layer pushes one angle forward.
Students miss home. Mums worry.
The guide shows the voice.
Short. Warm. A little cheeky.
The brand sections set the look.
Green. Cream. Warm serif. A steel tiffin.
The critic runs its five questions.
"Could any other kitchen say this?"
Most of the twenty fail right there.
"Delicious home food, delivered!" Dead.
"Taste of home, at your door!" Dead.
Three survive.
A human reads them out loud.
One makes the room laugh.
"Your mum called."
That one ships.
Then the human adds the last line.
p.s. call her back.
The model did not write that p.s.
It was the taste layer.
And now the guide has one more example.
Next time, the model knows p.s. lines can land.
That is one episode.
Twenty actions. One reward. One lesson saved.
Do that forty times and you have a brand.
Then you put it together.
This is the last step.
And it's where the forty pieces show up.
Everything hangs off one line.
One pot a day. Lock it tonight.
The website says it.
The apps say it.
The flyers say it.
The pamphlet says it.
The book says it, in its own way.
Even the tees say it.
Let me show you the pieces.
The website has a weekly rhythm.

attrs.alt: Pot, lock, drop. The weekly ritual.

content.text: Pot, lock, drop. The weekly ritual.
Sunday, the week's pots go out on WhatsApp.
Lock tomorrow's pot by 9pm.
It's cooked that morning.
Lunch pickup, or dinner delivery.
Then the week, day by day.
The idli pot. The paneer pot.
The pongal pot. The aloo pot.
Saturday is the party pot.
And Friday?
Friday, the pot rests.
That one line made me laugh.
It makes the whole thing feel human.
Like a real person runs it.
A tired, happy person who takes Fridays off.
You cannot ask a model for "human touches."
That prompt gives you slop.
You get human touches from an environment that rewards specifics.
"The pot rests" is a specific.
Then the flyers.
Five flyers. Stories, not ads.
Five A5 flyers. Each one a tiny story.
One is stamped confidential.
"These recipes were never meant to leave India."
"We smuggled them out in a tin of ghee."
One leans into having no shopfront.
"You'll never find us on a high street."
"No sign. No door. Just one pot a day."
And my favourite.
"Your mum called."
"She says you're not eating properly."
"We're handling it. £4.99."
And at the bottom: p.s. call her back.
That flyer is an insight wearing a joke.
Every Indian student in London has had that call.
It gets screenshotted.
Screenshots are free reach.
Free reach is a dense reward.
See how the layers stack in one A5 page?
The insight gave the story.
The guide gave the voice.
The brand sections gave the green and the serif.
The punish list kept out the discount badge.
The human kept the "p.s."
Then the pamphlet.

attrs.alt: One A4 page. Hand it to anyone.

content.text: One A4 page. Hand it to anyone.
One page.
Logo. Hero photo of idli and sambar in a steel tiffin.
The headline again.
How to order.
The week.
A QR code.
It has one job.
A neighbour should get the whole idea in ten seconds.
Print still works for local food.
Letterboxes. Office kitchens.
Temple and gurdwara notice boards.
A good one-pager beats a fancy site for this kind of reach.
The model would not have chosen print by itself.
The internet says print is dead.
The insight layer said otherwise.
Local food lives on paper.
Then the book.

attrs.alt: Pam's Kitchens of India. Thirteen plates.

content.text: Pam's Kitchens of India. Thirteen plates.
A thirty-one page coffee-table book.
Thirteen dishes. Thirteen places.
Vindaloo from Goa.
Biryani from Hyderabad.
Fish moilee from Kerala.
Masala chai from Assam and every street corner.
And one that made me grin.
Chicken tikka masala. Glasgow, via Punjab.
That is the voice.
Playful. True. A little nerdy.
Why make a book for a dark kitchen?
It turns food into culture.
It is a gift people give.
It is proof that the people behind it know their stuff.
Journalists love a book.
It is also the hardest test of the environment.
Thirty-one pages is a long episode.
Long episodes are where drift happens.
The colours stayed.
The voice stayed.
The steel and the green stayed.
That only happens if the layers hold.
Then the tees.
Tees, because why not.
Merch for a kitchen sounds silly.
It is also the cheapest billboard in London.
A good tee walks through a whole borough.
The tees carry the line, of course.
Tonal puff print on organic cotton.
Quiet enough to wear to work.
Loud enough that someone asks.
"Pam's Kitchen? What's that?"
That question is the whole point.
Now let me zoom out.
What did the RL framing actually buy us?
Three things.
First, a way to talk about slop.
Slop is reward hacking.
It is an agent chasing a cheap signal.
Once you see it that way, you can design against it.
You stop blaming the model.
You fix the environment.
Second, a way to scale taste.
Taste used to live in one person's head.
Now it lives in skill files, guides and a punish list.
The model reads them every time.
Taste becomes a property of the world.
Not a mood on a Tuesday.
Third, a way to connect craft to sales.
The dense rewards are craft signals.
Is it specific? Is it on brand?
Did someone screenshot it?
The sparse reward is money.
A good environment links them.
Every craft signal should point at a sale.
If it doesn't, cut it.
Fourth, compounding.
This is the sneaky one.
A normal brand project ends.
The agency hands over files.
The learning stops on that day.
An environment keeps learning.
Every kill adds a guide line.
Every street signal tunes the critic.
Every new piece starts smarter than the last.
The second flyer is better than the first.
The tenth is better than the second.
Not because anyone worked harder.
Because the world got a little wiser.
That is the part that makes me think this is real.
Most AI makes the first draft faster.
A good environment makes the hundredth draft better.
Speed is nice.
Getting better over time is the whole business.
Now the honest limits.
The RL picture is a metaphor stretched over real life.
Brands are not chess.
You cannot run a million episodes.
A kitchen gets maybe one episode a day.
One pot. One night of locks.
That is slow learning.
So you cheat, a little.
You run many cheap episodes in simulation.
Drafts. Mockups. Critic scores.
Then you run a few real episodes in the street.
Flyers. WhatsApp messages. Locked pots.
RL people call this the sim-to-real gap.
Things that score well in sim can flop in reality.
A flyer the critic loves might get ignored in a letterbox.
So the real-world signal always wins.
When the street disagrees with the critic, update the critic.
If I were running the first month, I'd watch a tiny dashboard.
Locks per night.
Locks per WhatsApp message sent.
Repeat lockers by week two.
Pamphlet QR scans, by street.
Screenshots and forwards, when people tell you.
Saturday party pot uptake.
None of these is sales on its own.
Each one is a breadcrumb toward sales.
And each one can feed back into the critic.
If the mum flyer drives locks, write more like it.
If the confidential one gets ignored, find out why.
That is the loop closing.
The street trains the critic.
The critic trains the drafts.
The drafts reach the street again.
Second limit.
Taste is still the bottleneck.
The model can draft forever.
Somebody has to say no.
If nobody says no, the environment fills with average.
Average is slop with better lighting.
Third limit.
Insights don't come from the model.
They come from living.
From talking to students who miss home food.
From watching a mum call her son twice in one evening.
You can give the agent your insights.
You cannot outsource having them.
And a fair objection.
"Isn't this just a brand book with extra steps?"
Kind of. Yes.
A brand book is a frozen environment.
Someone wrote it once.
Nobody updates it.
It sits in a drive folder.
New designers skim it on day one.
The RL version is alive.
It updates after every kill.
It has a critic that reads it every time.
It has rewards that point at money.
It has a punish list that grows.
A brand book tells you the rules.
An environment enforces them.
And learns new ones while it works.
So what is the model actually good for?
Speed, mostly.
It drafted forty pieces in the time a small studio might draft a handful.
It kept the rules better than a tired designer at 2am.
It never got bored of the brand book.
It made the hundredth dish story as carefully as the first.
That speed changes the economics.
A kitchen like this could never afford a full brand.
A book. A pamphlet. Five flyers. App shoots.
That used to be a five-figure agency job.
Now it's an environment and a few late nights.
That is the part that excites me.
Small businesses get a real brand.
Not a template.
Not a logo maker.
A world with rules, a voice and a reason to exist.
And the internet gets a little less sloppy.
Think about how you'd onboard a great new hire.
You wouldn't hand them a single prompt.
"Make our brand good. Go."
You'd sit them down.
You'd show them the best work.
You'd show them the worst work, and why.
You'd tell them the stories about customers.
You'd tell them the words we never use.
You'd check their first ten pieces closely.
Then the next fifty, less closely.
By month three, they just get it.
They have absorbed the environment.
That is exactly what the layers do for a model.
Skill files are the onboarding doc.
Guides are the portfolio review.
Insights are the customer stories.
The punish list is the banned words.
The critic is the senior designer.
You are the creative director.
The difference is speed.
A new hire takes three months.
The model takes an afternoon.
And it never forgets the onboarding.
This is also why I'm building what I'm building.
At ShopOS, we're building an AI lab that rolls up creative studios.
So that the internet isn't full of slop.
People hear that and think we want to replace studios.
It's the opposite.
A great studio is an environment.
Years of taste.
A sharp eye for what kills a piece.
A pile of guides nobody ever wrote down.
A gut for what will sell.
Most of that lives in a few heads.
When those people are tired, it slips.
When they leave, it walks out the door.
We want to write those environments down.
Skill files, guides, critics and punish lists.
Then put models inside them.
So the studio's taste runs at the speed of software.
And the humans spend their time on the hard calls.
The studio keeps its taste.
The internet gets fewer sad flyers.
Brands get work that sells.
Pam's Kitchen is a small version of that idea.
One kitchen. One environment. Forty pieces.
Let me give you the recipe in one go.
Start with nothing.
Which means start with your mess.
Look at it like a starting state.
What is the loudest problem?
Cut the action space.
Find the one idea that removes most choices.

I'll leave you with the question I started with.
What if a brand is an RL environment?
I think it already is.
Every brand is a world where actions get rewarded.
Most brands just never designed theirs.
So the loudest signal wins.
Clicks. Discounts. Noise.
Slop is just an environment nobody designed.
Design it, and the work changes.
The model stops guessing what you like.
It learns inside a world that already knows.

Forty pieces.
One voice.
